sentences.text: Gallimimus is a genus of dinosaur and represents the largest known member of the ornithomimid group.
Adult individuals measured about 6 meters in length, stood 1.9 meters high at the hip, and weighed between 400 and 490 kilograms.
The animal possessed a small, light head featuring large eyes that faced to the sides.
It was toothless, equipped with a keratinous beak, and had a delicate lower jaw.
It is highly likely that Gallimimus had feathers, a conclusion drawn from evidence found in its relative Ornithomimus.
Fossils were discovered by Polish-Mongolian expeditions in the Gobi Desert during the 1960s, with specific trips organized between 1963 and 1965.
The largest skeleton, which later became the holotype for Gallimimus bullatus, was discovered by Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska in 1964.
This large skeleton became the holotype—the specimen the species is based on—when the genus was formally described by Osmólska and colleagues in 1972.
Gallimimus was a fast-running animal that used its speed to escape predators, with an estimated running speed between 42 and 56 kilometers per hour.
It may have lived in groups, a hypothesis based on the discovery of multiple specimens in a bone bed.
It is debated whether Gallimimus used its beak structures for filter-feeding in water or for feeding on tough plant material as a herbivore.
The type species of the genus Gallimimus is Gallimimus bullatus, though Ornithomimus bullatus is considered a synonym of this name.
Gallimimus and related ornithomimosaurs lived during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago in the Maastrichtian, in what is now Asia.
The species lived from the Turonian to the Maastrichtian stages, spanning between 93.9 and 66 million years ago.

In 1988, Gregory S. Paul moved most ornithomimid species into the genus Ornithomimus, creating the combination O. bullatus. He later listed the species as Gallimimus (or Struthiomimus) bullatus in 2010 before reverting to Gallimimus in 2016. Most other paleontologists have kept the species involved in separate genera rather than grouping them under Ornithomimus.
Barsbold noted morphological variation among newer Gallimimus specimens, but this observation has never been published.
